Democratization of research refers to widening who can take part in science: how many researchers can participate in experimentation, and how easily they can generate and test hypotheses. In the context of [self-driving laboratories](/papers/topics/self-driving-laboratories/) it concerns how expensive automated experimental capability is shared, who is trained to build, maintain and use it, and how credit, data and standards are managed across many collaborators. Low-cost remote instruments such as Claude-Light ([kitchin2025b](/papers/kitchin2025b/)) are one practical route to broader access for teaching and prototyping.

## Centralized, distributed and hybrid SDL access (2025)

Canty et al. contrast centralized SDL facilities, which concentrate investment and staff and are accessed by application or fee (compared with CERN or the BioPACIFIC MIP), with distributed networks of group-level SDLs that pass jobs, information and materials among collaborators (compared with Galaxy Zoo, Foldit and the Harvard Clean Energy Project) ([Canty et al. 2025](/papers/canty2025/)). Centralized facilities offer high throughput per SDL, stability for funders and easier common protocols and certification, but address fewer research areas and may adapt slowly; distributed SDLs have lower setup costs and cover more areas but need much more coordination of data and standards. The authors favor hybrids, such as developing workflows on low-cost "frugal twin" systems before running them at a facility, or building instruments that plug into a facility. They also describe the workforce needed (developers, technicians and users), call for team science training and micro-credentials, and argue that funding should support shared infrastructure, for example through a consortium or institute for automated laboratory infrastructure. Summary: [canty2025](/papers/canty2025/).
